newsitem.title: UK: British rate rise fears ease at 11th hour.
newsitem.headline: British rate rise fears ease at 11th hour.

text.p: Financial markets scaled back their expectations of an imminent rise in Britain's 6.75 percent interest rates as the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee began its two-day meeting on Wednesday.
The committee's decision on whether to impose a fourth 1/4 point rise in as many months will be announced at 1100 GMT on Thursday.
"We've seen some softer data in the past few weeks and I think there's something of a reassessment of the chances of a rate rise," said CIBC chief economist David Coleman.

The swing in sentiment was most evident on the foreign exchanges, where sterling skidded down four pfennigs to below 3.02 deutschemarks and stumbled to near five month lows against the U.S. dollar at under 1.60.

But the equity market was sanguine amid hopes of a respite from the recent pattern of monthly rate rises. The Financial Times-Stock Exchange 100-share index breached the 5,000 level for the first time to a record 5,006.2.
A Reuters poll of 23 economists last week showed 16 expected a quarter-point rise in rates to 7.0 percent on Thursday.

But data released since then have shown a slowdown in the growth rate of narrow money supply -- a pointer to the strength of consumer spending -- less robust growth in the buoyant services sector and continued sluggishness in manufacturing.
"It's an extremely close call," Coleman said. "You can argue it convincingly either way, but I still think on balance they'll move tomorrow. But that will be it for a while."
Other economists are sceptical of the need for a further tightening of monetary policy at this stage.

"The Bank really hasn't got enough information on the third quarter yet," said SBC-Warburg UK economist Darren Winder. "It needs to take some time out to reassess. It can't keep raising interest rates by a quarter point every month -- that's not a credible policy."
Winder agrees with the market consensus which suggests the peak in interest rates will be around 7.5 percent, with rates remaining unchanged at that level for some time.
Some economists argue that the hawkish Bank of England has done enough to dampen inflationary pressures and should now wait to let the recent rate rises take effect.
A further tightening of the monetary screws risks boosting the pound even further and could push the already struggling manufacturing sector into recession.

However, the Bank has made clear it is worried about the inflationary potential of "windfall" gains totalling around 35 billion pounds ($56.9 billion), which millions of Britons are receiving this year as several building societies turn themselves into banks.

"There are no signs yet that higher rates are deterring demand," warned London Bond Broking's chief economist Stephen Lewis. He cited recent strong growth in retail sales as an argument for another rate rise to prevent the economy from overheating.
In May, Britain's new Labour government empowered the Bank of England to set interest rates.

Fears that the central bank could get the balance wrong and inadvertently push the economy into recession have gained credence after Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown failed to dampen consumer demand through higher taxes in his budget last month.
"The Bank has been left to sort it out with higher interest rates," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC.

"They have to steer a careful course and try not to over-react to some of the consumer spending data, which may be a one-off and could slow down anyway. Manufacturing is standing on one leg at the moment and they don't want to take that leg away."
The central bank will publish its quarterly inflation report, outlining its views on the chances of hitting the official 2.5 percent inflation target two years ahead, next week.
Now that the Bank has control of monetary policy, analysts say it needs to report the country is on course to meet the target -- otherwise it will look as if it is not carrying out its remit.
"It'll say we're on course but that the risks are skewed to the upside," said Winder. "That will give them room to put up rates again if they need to."
